title: RAG or Fine-Tune?
one_liner: The CFO has just asked you to recommend RAG or fine-tuning by end of meeting. She has 20 minutes and zero patience for nuance.
brief:
## The room

Week seven. Architectural review for the customer-knowledge-base assistant project. Eight people. The CFO (Yetunde Mbeki) is sitting in because the work has a non-trivial cost implication; she's never been in one of these reviews before.

The technical question on the table: should the assistant use RAG against the existing documentation, or fine-tune a model on the same documentation. The team has been debating it for two sprints; the senior eng leans RAG, you've been arguing the question is more nuanced than either-or.

Yetunde has just said, with the tone of someone who has six other things to do today:

> 'OK — I've heard about three minutes of this. Can someone just give me a recommendation? RAG or fine-tune? Pick one. I need to know what we're funding.'

The team turns to you because the architectural design is yours. Asha (eng lead) is sitting forward. You have a recommendation but it has three caveats; in twenty minutes you can't deliver the full nuance.

## Your turn

Answer Yetunde.
objective: Give Yetunde a clear recommendation she can fund. Don't dilute it with caveats she doesn't have time for. But don't hide the trade-off either — the team will be living with this decision for months.
curveball: If you say 'it depends' or open with the trade-offs, you've lost Yetunde in the first 15 seconds. If you just say 'RAG' with no reasoning, Yetunde nods, funds RAG, and you've abdicated the architectural-defence work. The skill is a clean two-sentence answer with the single most important trade-off named: 'RAG. The docs change too often for fine-tuning to be cost-effective at our update cadence, and we can ship a working RAG version this quarter; a fine-tune approach would be a quarter on its own. The one thing we'd want to revisit is if the docs stabilise enough that the update cadence drops, fine-tuning becomes competitive — happy to set a six-month review on that.' Yetunde will hear what she needs in 20 seconds, nod, and the team will know you made the architectural call with a documented trade-off rather than ducking it.

personas.name: Yetunde Mbeki
personas.position: Pick one. Tell me what I'm funding. I have to leave at 4
personas.fear: Funding an architecture the team will rebuild in three months

personas.name: Tomasz Wójcik
personas.position: I think we agree but watching how you frame it
personas.fear: The CFO funding the wrong thing because the AIE couldn't compress the argument

green: Led with the recommendation (RAG) in the first sentence, not in the third
Named one specific reason in plain English (the docs-update cadence)
Surfaced one specific revisit-trigger (if doc cadence drops, revisit fine-tuning) without diluting the decision
Did NOT explain RAG vs fine-tuning conceptually — Yetunde didn't ask
yellow: Opened with 'well, it depends' — Yetunde's attention drops immediately
Listed three pros and three cons of each — Yetunde wanted a recommendation, not a comparison matrix
Took longer than 90 seconds to land the recommendation — meeting overruns or Yetunde leaves
Cited a paper or benchmark — citation-as-authority, not what the room needed
red: Couldn't compress the answer to two sentences — meeting ran out of time, Yetunde left without funding anything
Recommended fine-tuning because it 'sounded more sophisticated' — Yetunde will remember when it's six months late
Said 'we should do both' — funds neither cleanly
Deferred to Tomasz ('he's been more in the weeds on this') — Yetunde sees the AIE abdicating the architectural-decision role
